newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 22.

text.p: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH -- BT AND BSKYB IN 500 MILLION
STG DIGITAL TV JOINT VENTURE

The finishing touches are being put to a 500 million stg digital television joint venture between British Telecom, BSkyB, Midland Bank and the Japanese electronics group, Matsushita, that could have decoders available by next Christmas. The plans have been submitted to the DTI and telecoms watchdog, Oftel. BT and BSkyB will each take 30 per cent with other partners taking 20 per cent.
-- CARLSON LIFTS INSPIRATIONS

US travel group, Carlson, is to come to the rescue of the trouble tour operator Inspirations, which delayed its results three times in the last week, by buying the 97 AT Mays travel shops it manages. The deal will inject funds into the group, whose capital adequacy is under investigation by the Civil Aviation Authority following two profit warnings in the autumn.
-- US MERGER SETS PACE AT AIRBUS

The merger of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas has led to the European partners in Airbus planning to sign a memorandum of understanding to transform the consortium into a limited company. The pact is vital for Airbus's proposed restructuring and will allow the planemaker to compete with Boeing in the new generation of super jumbo jets.
-- SHOPPERS CURB THE SPENDING SPREE

Claremont Garments, supplier to Marks and Spencer, has warned that sales are running below expectations, showing that retail spending in the run-up to Christmas may have slowed sharply. Shop chains believe the slowing pace of spending is due to Christmas Day falling in mid-week and will be made up in last minute purchases before Wednesday.
-- OFT CHIEF TO ORDER REPORT ON ACTUARIES

Director General of Fair Trading, John Bridgeman, is to launch an OFT investigation into actuaries. He believes actuaries could be acting against the public interest in a number of areas, including the methods they use to value company pension funds. He believes the methods could be short-changing workers who move jobs and ask for a transfer value for their pension contributions.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- BZW REBUKED OVER NORTHERN BID FEE

The US power group which is bidding for Northern Electric, CE Electric, is heading for a 782 million stg victory, after the Takeover Panel gave a rebuke to City investment bank BZW, who have also been banned from buying shares. The outcome of the takeover could still be in doubt if enough investors withdraw their acceptances while Northern has not ruled out a judicial review of the panel's decision to extend the bid for the second time in 24 hours.
-- BMW PLANS TO LINK ROVER WITH CHRYSLER

Owner of Rover Group, BMW, and America's third-largest carmaker, Chrysler, are negotiating to join forces to make cars in Britain and America. This could be a milestone in the modern history of the car industry, transforming the economics of the loss-making Rover car operations and securing the future of the Longbridge factory in Birmingham.
-- TOO CLEVER TO BE ECONOMISTS

Research by Bradford University suggests that too many qualifications are bad for you when it comes to economic forecasting. Economic forecasters with PhDs are 40 per cent less accurate than less qualified counterparts. However, some American-owned investment banks insist on doctorates for new economics recruits.
-- SALES HICCUP CASTS DOUBT OVER EARLY RATE RISE

Doubts have been raised about whether Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will have to lift interest rates early in the new year after the mixed news on the strength of pre-Christmas spending. Analysts say the figures, which show a record fall in unemployment and the strongest rise in real incomes since 1989, had increased the chances of a rate rise when Clarke meets governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George.
-- DTI MAY DROP FIGHT AGAINST GUNN AFTER SAUNDERS RULING

Prosecutors from the DTI are preparing to drop their bid to disqualify former chairman of collapsed British and Commonwealth financial group, John Gunn, due to a ruling on DTI transcripts by the European Court of Human Rights. Sources close to the DTI prosecution believe the ruling is the final blow to an action already in trouble.
THE OBSERVER
-- WATCHDOG PROBES NFC PENSION FUND

NFC, the privatised transport group, is being investigated by the pensions ombudsman following allegations that it has misused its pension fund surplus. The company is accused by former staff of using its 263 million stg pension fund surplus to boost profits by taking a 'holiday' from making payments into the fund.
-- BAA AWARDS ITSELF HEATHROW RAIL LINK

BAA is set to announce it has given itself the right to operate a second rail service linking central London to Heathrow, which will block Richard Branson's plan to run the rival train. BAA plans to launch the service in 1999.
-- THOUSANDS OF UNWARY COMPANIES DISREGARD NEW LEGISLATION AT THEIR PERIL

According to some pension advisers, thousands of small and medium-sized companies may face fines and legal sanctions for failing to comply with the Pensions Act. Almost 90 per cent of smaller companies contracted by Douglas Johnstone, the firm of advisors, have taken no advice and do not understand their obligations under the Act.
-- CAUTION PAYS OFF FOR CANNY KEN

According to business leaders, Government finances will be in better shape than predicted by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke in his Budget, putting the Tories in a strong position before the next general election. The Institute of Directors say that Clarke was too cautious when he revised down the 1996-97 public sector borrowing requirement forecast to 26.4 billion stg from 26.9 billion stg.
-- DIAMONDS ARE AN ADDICT'S BEST FRIEND

Study by De Beers suggests that the more diamonds one owns, the more one is driven to buy. The vice is particularly acute in Japan. In one year, 12 per cent of single-gem owners bought an extra diamond as compared with 53 per cent of people with five or more diamonds. The addiction is a new phenomenon and research shows it is getting worse with world-wide advertising.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- US UNIONS TO FIGHT BA MERGER

Airline unions in the US are set to launch a lobbying campaign against British Airway's merger with American Airlines. They will use Friday's appointment of Rodney Slater as Clinton's new Transport Secretary as the trigger for a co-ordinated campaign against the deal.
-- BURNFIELD BOSS SNUBS CHANCE TO MAKE 1.5 MILLION STG FROM BID

Non-executive chairman of Burnfield, the engineering firm facing a bid from Fairey Group, Brian McGowan, has turned down the chance of making 1.5 million stg by accepting the offer and has invested 630,000 stg of his personal fortune to back the company's rights issue.
-- OFFER PLANS POWER CODE
Stephen Littlechild, the electricity regulator, plans to introduce an enforceable code of practice for selling electricity services when he allows full competition in the market firms in 1998.
-- PIZZA MAN IN PAPER CHASE

Chairman of Pizza Express, Luke Johnson, is to join the struggling newspaper Sunday Business. He is a former media analyst at Kleinwort Benson and a columnist in the newspaper. He will invest up to 250,000 stg with a view to taking complete control by the middle of next year with a total investment of one million stg.
-- FEAR OVER MORGAN INQUIRY

The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation, the City watchdog, is to press ahead with disciplinary action against Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in the new year. Steps against fund manager Peter Young will be delayed until the Serious Fraud Office has revealed the results of its investigation.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- ARMCHAIR SHOPPING SHAKE-UP ON THE WAY

Home shopping is set to be transformed with the sale of Sears' subsidiary Freemans to Littlewoods. Littlewoods is convinced it needs the added market share to compete with Great Universal Stores. Further consolidation is likely as disappointed suitors for Freemans look for other acquisitions.
-- LABOUR'S BOOST FOR BUSINESS

Labour will unveil its first manifesto for small business in the New Year. Measures to aid high-tech firms and fledgling exporters will form key components of its Prospectus for Small Business. Labour plans to curb late payment and to remove red tape.
-- CABLE TV'S '100 MILLION STG HIDDEN BILL FOR ROADS'

According to research by Ulster University, taxpayers could face a 100 million stg repair bill for roads dug up by cable TV companies. The report claims that pipes carrying their fibre optic cable are likely to fail, thus causing subsidence.
-- L&G JOINS BATTLE FOR ANNUITIES

Legal and General is to pioneer higher annuity rates for people with small retirement funds. The move will signal its entry into the four billion stg-a-year pension annuities market. Chief executive David Posser believes people with small pension funds should have a better deal so that the smaller a pension fund is the higher the annuity rate L&G will pay.
-- SKYNET LOOKS FOR OFEX RETURN
Skynet Corporation is seeking a relisting on the unofficial Ofex market, despite an investigation into alleged share manipulation. BMC +44-171-377-1742
